{{short description|States that the algebra of n by n matrices satisfies a certain identity of degree 2n}}
In [[algebra]], the '''Amitsur–Levitzki theorem''' states that the algebra of ''n'' × ''n'' [[matrix (mathematics)|matrices]] over a [[commutative ring]] satisfies a certain identity of [[degree of a polynomial|degree]] 2''n''. It was [[mathematical proof|proved]] by {{harvs|txt|last=Amitsur|author1-link=Shimshon Amitsur|last2=Levitsky|author2-link=Jacob Levitzki|year=1950}}. In particular [[matrix ring]]s are [[polynomial identity ring]]s such that the smallest identity they satisfy has degree exactly 2''n''.

==Statement==
The '''standard polynomial''' of degree ''n'' is
<math display="block">S_n(x_1,\dots,x_n) = \sum_{\sigma\in S_{n}}\text{sgn}(\sigma)x_{\sigma(1)} \cdots x_{\sigma(n)} </math>
in non-commuting variables ''x''<sub>1</sub>, ..., ''x''<sub>''n''</sub>, where the sum is taken over all ''n''! elements of the [[symmetric group]] ''S''<sub>''n''</sub>.

The Amitsur–Levitzki theorem states that for ''n'' × ''n'' matrices ''A''<sub>1</sub>, ..., ''A''<sub>2''n''</sub> whose entries are taken from a commutative ring then

<math display="block">S_{2n}(A_1,\dots,A_{2n}) = 0.</math>

==Proofs==
{{harvs|txt|last=Amitsur|last2=Levitzki|year=1950}} gave the first proof.

{{harvtxt|Kostant|1958}} deduced the Amitsur–Levitzki theorem from the [[Koszul–Samelson theorem]] about primitive cohomology of [[Lie algebra]]s.

{{harvtxt|Swan|1963}} and {{harvtxt|Swan|1969}} gave a simple [[combinatorial]] proof as follows. By linearity it is enough to prove the theorem when each matrix has only one nonzero entry, which is 1. In this case each matrix can be encoded as a directed edge of a [[directed graph|graph]] with ''n'' vertices. So all matrices together give a graph on ''n'' vertices with 2''n'' directed edges. The identity holds provided that for any two vertices ''A'' and ''B'' of the graph, the number of odd [[Eulerian path]]s from ''A'' to ''B'' is the same as the number of even ones. (Here a path is called odd or even depending on whether its edges taken in order give an [[odd and even permutations|odd or even permutation]] of the 2''n'' edges.) Swan showed that this was the case provided the number of edges in the graph is at least 2''n'', thus proving the Amitsur–Levitzki theorem.

{{harvtxt|Razmyslov|1974}} gave a proof related to the [[Cayley–Hamilton theorem]].

{{harvtxt|Rosset|1976}} gave a short proof using the [[exterior algebra]] of a [[vector space]] of [[dimension (vector space)|dimension]] 2''n''.

{{harvtxt|Procesi|2015}} gave another proof, showing that the Amitsur–Levitzki theorem is the Cayley–Hamilton identity for the generic Grassman matrix.{{clarify|needs definition if this term is being used (also it should be "Grassmann" but the original paper consistently misspells this as well)|date=September 2026}} Claudio Procesi's proof used a similar technique to Rosset but is presented in a way that could make the theorem more easily transferrable to other problems. A principal property used in this proof is antisymmetry to convert a multilinear expression to an antisymmetric one.
